Nursing Department Guidelines
Nursing Care Standards
●
Every inpatient has an individualized nursing care plan developed within the first shift after admission.
●
Vital signs are checked per the frequency set by the attending physician, with a minimum of once
every 8 hours for stable patients.
●
Nurses document care using the standard nursing notes format at every shift.
Shift Handover
●
Handover between shifts uses the SBAR format and occurs at the patient's bedside whenever
possible.
●
Outstanding tasks, pending results, and any safety concerns must be explicitly communicated at
handover.
Nurse-to-Patient Ratios
●
General wards maintain a target ratio of 1 nurse to 6 patients per shift.
●
Intensive Care Units maintain a target ratio of 1 nurse to 2 patients per shift.
Infection Control
●
Hand hygiene is performed before and after every patient contact, following the WHO 'Five Moments
for Hand Hygiene'.

●
Personal protective equipment (PPE) is used according to the patient's isolation precautions (contact,

Pharmacy Department Guidelines
Role of the Pharmacy Department
●
The pharmacy reviews, dispenses, and monitors all medications ordered for inpatients and
outpatients.
●
A licensed pharmacist reviews every new medication order for appropriateness, dosing, and
interactions before it is dispensed.
Dispensing Process
●
Inpatient medications are dispensed through a unit-dose system, with each dose individually packaged
and labeled.
●
Outpatient prescriptions require a valid prescription from a registered physician and are verified
against the patient's known allergies.
●
Controlled substances (e.g., opioids) require additional documentation and are tracked in a separate
controlled-drug register.
Medication Safety Checks
●
The pharmacy system automatically flags drug-drug interactions, duplicate therapy, and allergy
conflicts.
●
High-alert medications require pharmacist counter-verification before release to the ward.

Billing Department Information
Billing Process Overview
●
Charges accumulate automatically in the patient's account as services, medications, and procedures
are provided.
●
The billing office verifies insurance coverage or payment arrangements at admission and again at
discharge.
Payment Methods
●
Accepted payment methods include cash, debit/credit card, bank transfer, and approved insurance
panels.
●
Patients with panel insurance must present a valid insurance card; the billing office coordinates
pre-authorization where required.
Discharge Billing
●
A final itemized bill is prepared once the discharging physician signs the discharge order.
●
Patients or their families may request an itemized breakdown of all charges before making final
payment.
Billing Disputes
●
Any disputed charge is reviewed by the billing office within 5 working days, with the patient notified of
the outcome in writing.

Patient Registration Process
New Patient Registration
●
New patients provide full name, date of birth, CNIC/passport number, contact details, and next of kin
information.
●
The registration system generates a unique Medical Record Number (MRN) used across all hospital
departments.
●
A photo may be taken at registration for identity verification, consistent with hospital privacy policy.
Returning Patient Registration
●
Returning patients are located in the system by MRN, CNIC, or name plus date of birth.
●
Any changes to contact information, insurance, or next of kin are updated at each visit.
Registration Channels
●
Walk-in registration desks in the main lobby and outpatient clinics.
●
Online pre-registration through the hospital website for scheduled appointments.
●
Phone registration for patients arranging admission in advance.
Data Privacy at Registration
●
All personal and medical information collected at registration is protected under the hospital's privacy

Data Privacy at Registration
●
All personal and medical information collected at registration is protected under the hospital's privacy
and data protection policy.
●
Staff may only access patient records relevant to the patient's current care (minimum necessary
access principle).

Patient Admission Guidelines
Types of Admission
●
Elective Admission: scheduled in advance for planned procedures or treatment, arranged through the
outpatient clinic.
●
Emergency Admission: initiated from the ED for patients who need inpatient care (see
emergency_procedures.pdf).
●
Direct Admission: a patient is admitted on a physician's order without going through the ED, usually for
a known condition requiring monitoring.
Admission Requirements
●
A valid CNIC or other government ID is required for registration.
●
An admitting physician's order, including provisional diagnosis and requested ward/bed type, must be
on file.
●
Insurance or payment method is verified by the billing office before or shortly after admission (see
billing_information.pdf).
●
A signed general consent for treatment is obtained from the patient or their legal guardian.
Bed Allocation
●
Bed allocation is coordinated by the Bed Management Office based on clinical need, ward specialty,
and isolation requirements.

Bed Allocation
●
Bed allocation is coordinated by the Bed Management Office based on clinical need, ward specialty,
and isolation requirements.
●
Patients requiring isolation (e.g., infectious disease) are prioritized for single rooms where available.
Admission Documentation Checklist
●
Complete nursing admission assessment within 2 hours of arrival on the ward.
●
Physician's admission note documented within 24 hours.
●
Allergy status confirmed and allergy wristband applied.
●
Initial care plan and expected length of stay documented.

Emergency Triage Protocol
Purpose of Triage
●
Triage is the process of quickly sorting patients by the severity of their condition so the sickest patients
are treated first.
●
Shifa International Hospitals uses a 4-level triage system based on the Emergency Severity Index
(ESI) model.
Triage Levels
●
Level 1 – Critical: immediate life threat (e.g., cardiac arrest, severe airway obstruction). Seen
immediately, no waiting.
●
Level 2 – Emergent: high risk situation, unstable vitals, or severe pain (e.g., chest pain, stroke
symptoms). Seen within 10 minutes.
●
Level 3 – Urgent: stable but needs several resources (e.g., moderate abdominal pain, fractures). Seen
within 30-60 minutes.
●
Level 4 – Non-urgent: minor complaints needing one resource or less (e.g., minor cuts, cold
symptoms). Seen within 60-120 minutes.
Triage Nurse Responsibilities
●
Record chief complaint, vital signs, allergies, and current medications.

Triage Nurse Responsibilities
●
Record chief complaint, vital signs, allergies, and current medications.
●
Assign the ESI level and communicate it clearly to the receiving team using the color-coded triage
board (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green).
●
Re-triage any patient whose condition changes while waiting.
Special Situations
●
Pediatric, obstetric, and psychiatric emergencies follow the same 4-level system but are flagged for the
relevant on-call specialist immediately after triage.
●
Mass casualty events trigger the hospital's Emergency Preparedness Plan, which temporarily
overrides normal triage staffing ratios.

Emergency Department – General Care Guidelines
Scope of the Emergency Department (ED)
●
The ED at Shifa International Hospitals provides 24/7 care for acute illness, trauma, and
life-threatening conditions.
●
All patients arriving by ambulance or self-presenting are registered at the ED reception desk before
clinical assessment, except in immediately life-threatening cases where treatment begins first.
●
The department is staffed by emergency physicians, ED nurses, and on-call specialists from Surgery,
Medicine, Pediatrics, and Cardiology.
Levels of Emergency Care
●
Resuscitation Bay: for cardiac arrest, severe trauma, and airway emergencies. Response time target
is immediate.
●
Acute Care Area: for patients needing continuous monitoring but who are not in immediate danger of
death.
●
Ambulatory Care Area: for minor injuries and stable, low-acuity complaints such as sprains or minor
lacerations.

Standard Operating Principles
●
Every patient is assessed within 10 minutes of arrival by a triage nurse (see emergency_triage.pdf for
the full triage protocol).
●
Vital signs (blood pressure, pulse, temperature, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate) are recorded on
arrival and repeated per the acuity level.
●
A consulting physician must document a clear management plan in the patient's chart before any
admission or discharge decision.
●
All emergency medications are administered only after verification of patient identity using two
identifiers (name and MRN/CNIC).
Discharge from the ED
●
Patients discharged from the ED receive written aftercare instructions and a follow-up plan.
●
Any patient leaving against medical advice (LAMA) must sign a documented LAMA form after being
counseled on the risks.

Emergency Admission & Escalation Procedures
Admitting an Emergency Patient
●
Step 1: Patient is triaged and assigned an ESI level (see emergency_triage.pdf).
●
Step 2: The attending ED physician performs an assessment and orders any needed labs or imaging.
●
Step 3: If admission is required, the physician contacts the relevant department (e.g., Cardiology,
General Surgery) for a bed and hand-over.
●
Step 4: Nursing staff complete the admission checklist, including allergy bands, consent forms, and
initial nursing assessment.
●
Step 5: The patient is transferred to the ward or ICU with a full handover summary.
Escalation of Care
●
Any patient who deteriorates (drop in oxygen saturation, altered consciousness, unstable vitals)
triggers a Rapid Response Team (RRT) call.
●
The RRT includes a senior physician, an ICU nurse, and a respiratory therapist, and must respond
within 5 minutes of being paged.
●
All RRT activations are logged and reviewed weekly by the Patient Safety Committee.

Inter-Hospital Transfers
●
Patients requiring a level of care not available on-site (e.g., specialized neurosurgery) are stabilized
first, then transferred with a full medical summary and consent.
●
A transfer is never initiated until the receiving facility has confirmed bed availability.

Patient Safety Risk Assessment Guidelines
Purpose
●
Risk assessments identify patients who are more likely to experience an adverse event, so preventive
steps can be taken early.
Fall Risk Assessment
●
Every inpatient is screened on admission using the Morse Fall Scale, which scores history of falling,
secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, IV therapy, gait, and mental status.
●
Patients scoring 'high risk' receive a yellow wristband, a bed alarm, and a bedside fall-prevention sign.
●
Reassessment occurs after any fall, transfer, or significant change in condition.
Pressure Injury Risk Assessment
●
The Braden Scale is used to assess risk of pressure injuries (bedsores) for all patients with limited
mobility.
●
High-risk patients receive a turning schedule every 2 hours and a pressure-relieving mattress.
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) Risk Assessment
●
All adult inpatients are assessed for VTE risk within 24 hours of admission using a standardized
scoring tool.
●

●
All adult inpatients are assessed for VTE risk within 24 hours of admission using a standardized
scoring tool.
●
Appropriate prophylaxis (mechanical or pharmacological) is prescribed based on the risk score, unless
contraindicated.
Documentation
●
All risk assessment scores and the resulting care plan must be documented in the patient's chart and
reviewed at every shift change.

Patient Safety Toolkit
Core Patient Safety Goals
●
Correctly identify every patient using two identifiers before any procedure, medication, or transfusion.
●
Improve communication among caregivers, especially during shift handovers, using the SBAR format
(Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation).
●
Reduce the risk of healthcare-associated infections through hand hygiene compliance at all five WHO
moments.
●
Reduce the risk of harm from falls by screening every inpatient with a validated fall-risk tool on
admission.
Medication Safety
●
High-alert medications (insulin, heparin, opioids, concentrated electrolytes) require an independent
double-check by a second nurse before administration.
●
All verbal orders must be read back and confirmed before being carried out.
●
Look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) drugs are stored separately and labeled with tall-man lettering.
Incident Reporting
●
Any near-miss, adverse event, or sentinel event must be reported through the hospital's electronic

Incident Reporting
●
Any near-miss, adverse event, or sentinel event must be reported through the hospital's electronic
incident reporting system within 24 hours.
●
Reports are reviewed without individual blame, focusing on system-level causes, in line with a 'just
culture' approach.
Surgical Safety
●
The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist is completed at three points: before anesthesia (sign-in), before
incision (time-out), and before the patient leaves the operating room (sign-out).

Patient Rights & Responsibilities
Patient Rights
●
Right to receive care with dignity, respect, and without discrimination.
●
Right to receive clear information about diagnosis, treatment options, and expected costs.
●
Right to give or refuse informed consent for any procedure or treatment.
●
Right to privacy and confidentiality of personal health information.
●
Right to request a second opinion or to be referred to another facility.
Patient Responsibilities
●
Provide accurate and complete information about health history and current condition.
●
Follow the agreed treatment plan or discuss concerns with the care team before deviating from it.
●
Treat hospital staff and other patients with courtesy and respect.
●
Meet financial obligations for the services received, as outlined by the billing office.
Complaints & Feedback
●
Patients or families may submit complaints or feedback through the Patient Relations Office, in person,
by phone, or via the hospital website.
